issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of natural disaster. Generic sensory cues can fit disaster trauma, but snakes and babies are highly specific cues with no clear link to a natural disaster and, taken together with body odour, suggest unrelated trigger themes rather than a single trauma network.

Within the overall profile, the memory/appraisal content is also mismatched. 'Intense shame on recall' usually implies a strong negative appraisal/self-evaluative theme, yet no Negative Appraisals items are endorsed and that node is formulation-wise disconnected. For a natural disaster survivor, shame can occur, but as the only explicit meaning-based memory item it sits awkwardly with otherwise cue-driven fragmented recall and no corresponding appraisal content.

'Babies' as an auditory trigger is hard to reconcile with a natural-disaster trauma in this profile unless there is specific undisclosed trauma content involving infants; the other triggers (loud noises, sweat/body odour) are more disaster-congruent, so this item stands out as clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking conflict/create drama' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The formulation links triggers mainly with memory and only minimally with maladaptive strategies, and the other selected items suggest intrusive sensory recall rather than an anger/interpersonal-dysregulation pattern. This coping item appears to target a symptom style not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: 'Sexual coping' is likewise poorly supported by the rest of the profile. With no threat or negative appraisal content selected and memory items focused on fragmentation/triggered recall, this strategy lacks a clear cognitive-affective anchor in the chosen profile and is difficult to connect specifically to natural-disaster PTSD here.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, sweat/body odour and alcohol smell are hard to link plausibly as primary trauma reminders unless there is additional disaster-specific context (e.g., shelter crowding, intoxicated bystanders). Loud noises fit, but these two olfactory triggers are clinically difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

Intense shame on recall is not impossible after a natural disaster, but as the only affective memory item here it is a poor fit with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes sensory triggering and fragmented involuntary recall rather than self-blame, humiliation, or morally charged memory content. This makes the memory node less coherent with the trauma type and the selected triggers/strategies.

Alcohol smell is a hard-to-explain trigger for a natural-disaster trauma in the absence of any matching trauma context or linked appraisal content; loud noise and smoke are coherent disaster-related cues, but alcohol odor stands out as clinically implausible here.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Intense shame on recall is not impossible after a natural disaster, but with no negative-appraisal content and no other memory material suggesting shame-linked actions or moral failure, this item is poorly supported and clinically discordant with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Alcohol Use: drink alcohol
issues.explanation: Using alcohol can occur nonspecifically, but paired with an alcohol-smell trigger it implies trauma meaning centered on alcohol-related cues that is not represented elsewhere in the disaster-based trigger or memory profile, reducing coherence.

vignette:
Mateo had always found a clean, quiet satisfaction in the sterile precision of the operating theatre. For fifteen years as a surgeon, his world was one of control, of problems that could be cut away, of bodies that could, with skill and focus, be repaired. That sense of order was incinerated over the course of a single weekend six months ago. He and his wife had been staying in a remote cabin when the wildfire came. It moved with an unnatural speed, a roaring beast that consumed the forest. What he remembers most are the sounds of trees cracking like gunshots and the thick, acrid smell of burning pine that clung to everything, a smell that felt like the world itself was being rendered down to ash.

In the weeks that followed, the fire came home with him. The city was full of traps. A car backfiring on the street outside his home would instantly plunge him back into the chaos, not as a full narrative, but as a sensory fragment: the percussive blast of a propane tank exploding at a nearby property. These moments, which could be triggered by any loud, sudden noise, were not just frightening; they brought with them a profound and overwhelming grief for a world that had felt safe just moments before the fire. He felt as though he was only remembering parts of what happened, with the rest of it lost in a fog of smoke and panic, a sensation that was deeply unsettling for a man who prided himself on memory and meticulousness.

The memories themselves became a source of threat. After a flashback, often arriving without warning while he was driving or trying to read, he would be left raw and hyper-alert for hours. The lingering image of the orange sky would prime his senses, and he would find himself subtly sniffing the air for the slightest hint of smoke, his ears straining to catch any sharp noise that might signal a repeat of the danger. This vigilance made it almost inevitable that he would encounter another trigger, locking him into a cycle where the memory of the threat and the cues for that threat began to feed one another, making his world feel progressively smaller and more dangerous.

This escalating sense of siege began to bleed into his work. During a routine cholecystectomy, the familiar smell of the cauterizing pen-a sharp, burnt scent he had registered thousands of times without a thought-suddenly became the smell of the fire. A wave of panic washed over him. Though his hands remained steady, his focus fractured. He finished the procedure on pure muscle memory, his mind a world away. That evening, he went straight for the whiskey, pouring a glass to blunt the sharp edges of his anxiety. He then spent hours scrolling through his phone, a frantic attempt to distract himself from the echoes of the day. This pattern became his default response; whenever the world ambushed him with a trigger, he would retreat into alcohol or a flurry of mindless activity to push the experience away.

His attempts to suppress the memories seemed only to make them more disjointed. The more he used alcohol to escape, the more he reinforced the feeling that the memory was an incomplete picture, a series of terrifying snapshots he couldn't assemble into a coherent story. His wife noticed his withdrawal, the way he would sometimes initiate sex with a desperate, detached urgency, using the physical sensation as another form of release from the tension that was constantly thrumming beneath his skin. The intimacy they had shared for over a decade began to feel like another casualty of the fire, leaving him more isolated with the fragments of his memory.

Mateo finally sought help after a fire alarm test at the hospital triggered a flashback so vivid he completely lost his train of thought while briefing a junior resident. The momentary blankness, the loss of his professional command, terrified him more than the memory itself. He is haunted by the belief that the memory is broken, that he is missing a crucial piece of the story that would allow it to settle. What brought him to therapy was the dawning fear that this internal chaos could one day cause him to make a mistake, to bring the fire's destructive power into the one place he had always felt completely in control.
